solution_overview:
A hospital reviewed patient charts for three risk factors: Hypertension ($H$), Diabetes ($D$), and Obesity ($O$). We are given the probabilities of these events and their intersections. We can summarize the given information:

$$P(H) = 0.45$$
$$P(D) = 0.25$$
$$P(O) = 0.38$$
$$P(H \cap D) = 0.14$$
$$P(H \cap O) = 0.20$$
$$P(D \cap O) = 0.12$$
$$P(H \cap D \cap O) = 0.07$$

These values will be used to calculate probabilities of various combinations of risk factors. A common approach for this type of problem involves the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

The probability that a patient has at least one risk factor is the probability of the union of the three events, $P(H \cup D \cup O)$. For three events, the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion states:

$$P(H \cup D \cup O) = P(H) + P(D) + P(O) - P(H \cap D) - P(H \cap O) - P(D \cap O) + P(H \cap D \cap O)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(H \cup D \cup O) = 0.45 + 0.25 + 0.38 - 0.14 - 0.20 - 0.12 + 0.07$$
$$P(H \cup D \cup O) = 1.08 - 0.46 + 0.07$$
$$P(H \cup D \cup O) = 0.62 + 0.07$$
$$P(H \cup D \cup O) = 0.69$$

The probability is $0.69$, or $69\%$. The claim states this is above $70\%$. Since $0.69 \not> 0.70$, the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The probability of having exactly one risk factor means a patient has only Hypertension, or only Diabetes, or only Obesity, but not any combination. This can be calculated from the given probabilities using the formula:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(H) + P(D) + P(O) - 2P(H \cap D) - 2P(H \cap O) - 2P(D \cap O) + 3P(H \cap D \cap O)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.45 + 0.25 + 0.38 - 2(0.14) - 2(0.20) - 2(0.12) + 3(0.07)$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.08 - 0.28 - 0.40 - 0.24 + 0.21$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 1.08 - 0.92 + 0.21$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.16 + 0.21$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.37$$

This probability is $0.37$, or $37\%$. The claim states this exceeds $38\%$. Since $0.37 \not> 0.38$, the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The probability of having exactly two risk factors means the patient has, for example, Hypertension and Diabetes, but not Obesity; or Hypertension and Obesity, but not Diabetes; or Diabetes and Obesity, but not Hypertension. This is computed by summing the pairwise intersections and subtracting the triple intersection three times to remove cases where all three factors are present:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(H \cap D) + P(H \cap O) + P(D \cap O) - 3P(H \cap D \cap O)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.14 + 0.20 + 0.12 - 3(0.07)$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.46 - 0.21$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.25$$

This probability is $0.25$, or $25\%$. The claim states this is at least $26\%$. Since $0.25 \not\ge 0.26$, the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The probability that a patient has none of the three risk factors is the complement of having at least one risk factor. That is, $P(	ext{none}) = 1 - P(H \cup D \cup O)$. We calculated $P(H \cup D \cup O)$ in Part A:

$$P(\text{none}) = 1 - 0.69$$
$$P(\text{none}) = 0.31$$

This probability is $0.31$, or $31\%$. The claim states this is under $30\%$. Since $0.31 \not< 0.30$, the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The probability that a patient has at least two risk factors means the patient has exactly two risk factors OR exactly three risk factors. These are mutually exclusive outcomes, so their probabilities can be added directly:

$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(\text{exactly three})$$

From Part C, we found $P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.25$. The probability of exactly three risk factors is directly given as $P(H \cap D \cap O) = 0.07$. Adding these values:

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.25 + 0.07$$
$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.32$$

This probability is $0.32$, or $32\%$. The claim states this is above $30\%$. Since $0.32 > 0.30$, the statement is True.
